claims.text: Visioning should start where the customer is. Some customers arrive with a list of AI ideas. Others have no list at all. Each needs a different path through the session.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: The customer has a use case list. Validate and prioritize it. Spend most of the session completing the use case fields: persona, workflow, pain, data sources, impact and effort rationale, and uncertainties. Then negotiate placement on the impact/effort 2x2. The customer has no list. Bring an informed hypothesis and relevant departmental examples, then draw out real workflows tied to outcomes. Glean's Blueprint material provides sample department 2x2s for this. Sometimes you will need a mini Visioning session with each department to understand its priorities.

claims.text: "What could AI do for you?" invites vague wishes. Use departmental thought starters and focused questions about recurring work instead. Ask what takes time, what goes wrong, and what the consequence is.

claims.text: Example use cases help customers recognize their own work. They do not prove that a use case is feasible or valuable for this customer. Don't replace listening with a tour of a use case catalog. Tip If you show examples, present a few that are relevant to the department in the room and say plainly that they are there to be changed, merged, or discarded.

claims.text: Finance, ten workflows: clarify each one, cluster duplicates, complete the use case fields, and prioritize on the 2x2. Spend the time on evidence and ranking, not idea generation. Legal, no list: bring outcome-led hypotheses and two or three relevant examples, such as finding the approved clause language for a contract type. Then draw out the team's actual jobs to be done and the evidence for each, such as frequency, time taken, and consequences.

claims.text: Visioning time goes quickly. A timed agenda with visible checkpoints keeps the session on track toward its decisions.

claims.text: Welcome and purpose | 5 | Shared understanding of the decision the group will make Context and outcomes | 10 | Business goals confirmed in the customer's words Opportunity discovery | 20 | Candidate workflows captured in the use case log Prioritization | 20 | Impact/effort placement and rationale agreed Commitments | 5 | Owners, next steps, and Day-in-the-Life participants This timing is the course's recommended default. It sits within the ranges in Glean's Visioning playbook, which allows 10–15 minutes for context, 15–20 for discovery, 15–20 for prioritization, and 5 for recap and next steps.

claims.text: Durations differ across Glean sources. When you have less time, cut scope deliberately: cover fewer departments, pre-populate the list from pre-work, and shorten context. Always keep prioritization and the owner and next-step commitments. Without them, the session produces no decision. If you can't complete enough discovery properly, schedule a second session rather than rushing.

claims.text: Open by explaining the decision the group will make together: which few workflows deserve deeper discovery, and why. Then confirm the business goals in the customer's language. Glean's Visioning playbook asks for an open, consultative, strategic tone, and warns against checklist-style or interrogative discovery.

claims.text: Useful questions from Glean's discovery bank include: "What are your team's core responsibilities and KPIs?" "How is success measured, for you and for your team?" "What recurring challenges or bottlenecks reduce efficiency or cause risk?" "Can you recall a recent workflow that took longer than it should have?" Reflect the answer back before you explore solutions: "So the priority this quarter is faster onboarding for new hires, and the friction is finding the right procedure across three systems. Is that right?"

claims.text: "Would our agent save you hours?" is a leading question. It invites a polite yes and produces no evidence. In your notes, keep three things separate: what the customer observed, what they hope for, and what the facilitator hypothesizes.

claims.text: Glean's onboarding training encourages a strategic conversation about what amazing would look like for the business, not only what good looks like. Ask leaders to describe the outcome a year from now if this went exceptionally well. Their answer gives you the outcome language, and often the metric, for everything that follows. Product-led Outcome-led Which Glean features interest you? Where does your team lose time today, and what does it cost? Would an AI assistant help? What would amazing look like here a year from now? Do you want agents? Which decisions or handoffs slow this work down?

claims.text: Don't settle impact and effort on the facilitator's opinion. Ask users, business owners, and technical owners for the evidence behind each rating. claims.text: The output of Visioning is a list of prioritized use cases, placed on a table and an impact/effort 2x2, that tells you which teams to meet for Day-in-the-Life interviews. Read the list aloud so everyone hears the same thing. Assign provisional impact and effort ratings, with a rationale for each. Place each row on the matrix. Discuss the disputed assumptions. These are the rows where people disagree. Ask the sponsor or champion: "Does this reflect where we should start?"

claims.text: Glean sources recommend a small first wave, described as three to four hero use cases in one place and three to five priorities in another. Size the wave to the interview capacity you actually have. High-impact, lower-effort use cases are your quick wins. A selected high-impact, higher-effort item can be a strategic bet that deserves deeper discovery. Partner guidance warns against prioritizing complexity, such as slow, hard-to-ship multi-system agents, for initial deployments.

claims.text: Glean's onboarding training describes the impact/effort matrix as the tool that stops a customer's wishlist from being treated as equally important. The training also describes placing items on the matrix as a kind of negotiation with the customer about where to spend effort first. claims.text: Glean's Visioning playbook asks you to share session notes, the prioritized use case table, and next steps with all attendees within 24 hours. A strong recap includes: The purpose of the session, in one line. Three to five key takeaways. The prioritized use cases, with a short rationale. A summary of quick wins and strategic bets. Actions, with owners and dates, including the DITL sessions. Open assumptions for participants to correct. Attach the editable use case log and a snapshot of the matrix, not just a deck.
